mcqs.question: A value has properties `{ x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }` and is passed (via a variable, not a literal) to a function expecting a `Point` interface with only `x` and `y`. Does TypeScript accept it, and why?
options: No, because `z` is an extra property not declared on `Point`
Yes — TypeScript is structurally typed, so a value only needs to have at least the properties a type requires, regardless of its declared type or extra properties
No, because the value was never explicitly declared as type `Point`
Yes, but only because TypeScript silently strips the extra `z` property at runtime
mcqs.explanation: Structural typing checks shape, not declared name — a value satisfies `Point` as long as it has compatible `x` and `y` properties, and extra properties like `z` are simply ignored for the check. Nothing is stripped at runtime; TypeScript's checking is purely compile-time and the object is passed through unchanged.

options: It only needs a `name` property; `age` is optional
It needs either a `name` property or an `age` property, but not necessarily both
It needs neither property, since intersections are only used for documentation and aren't enforced
It needs both a `name` property and an `age` property — an intersection requires every constituent type's shape at once
mcqs.explanation: An intersection type (`&`) combines requirements — a value must satisfy every constituent type simultaneously, so `Person` needs both `name` and `age`. "Either/or" describes a union (`|`), not an intersection, and intersections are fully enforced by the type checker, not just documentation.

options: `result` is `string | undefined` with the generic version; with the `any` version it would be typed `any`, so calling a nonexistent method on it would compile without error
`result` is `string | undefined` either way — generics and `any` provide identical safety here
`result` is `any` in both versions, since arrays always lose their element type in TypeScript
The generic version requires explicitly writing `firstElement<string>(...)` — it cannot be inferred from the array argument
mcqs.explanation: The generic version infers `T` as `string` from the argument, giving `result` the precise type `string | undefined`. The `any`-typed version would give `result` type `any`, silently allowing any property or method access to type-check even if it doesn't exist at runtime — exactly the guarantee generics preserve and `any` discards. TypeScript can infer `T` from the call; an explicit type argument isn't required here.

mcqs.question: A function parameter is typed `any`, and its value is assigned to a local variable elsewhere in the codebase with no explicit type annotation. What happens to that local variable's type?
options: It becomes `any` too, silently — `any` propagates to anything assigned from it, with no warning at the point of assignment
TypeScript infers its type from how it's later used in the code
It's rejected at compile time, since assigning from `any` to an untyped variable is an error
It defaults to `unknown`, requiring a check before further use
mcqs.explanation: `any` is contagious: any value assigned from an `any`-typed source becomes `any` as well, with no compile error marking the point where safety was lost — which is exactly why a single `any` deep in a call chain can erase type checking for everything downstream. TypeScript doesn't retroactively infer a narrower type from later usage, doesn't reject the assignment, and doesn't default to `unknown` on its own — that's a deliberate, different type you'd have to choose explicitly.

options: Because `data` is declared as optional on both branches of the union
Because TypeScript narrows the union based on the `ok` discriminant — only the `{ ok: true; data: T }` branch has a `data` property, and checking `result.ok` proves which branch applies
Because `ApiResult` is a generic type, and generics always require an explicit type guard before any property access
It isn't actually restricted — `result.data` would also compile fine outside the `if` block
mcqs.explanation: `ApiResult<T>` is a discriminated union — checking the `ok` field lets TypeScript narrow which of the two object shapes applies, and only the `ok: true` branch declares `data`. This has nothing to do with `data` being optional, and it isn't a generic-specific rule; accessing `result.data` outside the guard would indeed fail to compile since `data` doesn't exist on the `ok: false` branch.

TypeScript applies an excess property check specifically to object literals passed or assigned directly, as a safety net against typos — assigning through a variable first bypasses this stricter check
`coords` has fewer properties than the literal, so it satisfies `Point` more precisely

mcqs.explanation: TypeScript's excess property check is a narrow, deliberate exception applied only to object literals given directly at the call site — it exists specifically to catch typo'd property names. Passing the same shape via a variable is checked under ordinary structural typing rules, which allow extra properties, so it passes. Both TypeScript's literal check and its general structural rules apply to all values equally otherwise — there's no separate "nominal" mode for variables, and `coords` has exactly the same properties as the literal.
